title: Interrupts, IRQLs and Scheduling
summary: Hardware demands attention at any moment through **interrupts**, and the kernel must decide what can interrupt what. Windows does this with **interrupt request levels** (IRQLs). The IRQL a piece of code runs at decides what it may do: whether it can wait, touch paged memory, or be preempted. This lesson explains the levels, **DPCs**, **spin locks**, and the rules that cause the most famous blue screen of all.
markdown:
## Interrupts When a device needs the processor (a network packet arrived, a disk read finished, a key was pressed) it raises an **interrupt**. The processor stops what it is doing, saves enough state to resume, and runs the driver's **interrupt service routine** (ISR). A clock also interrupts regularly, which is how the scheduler gets control to switch threads (lesson 6.05). But an interrupt can arrive while the kernel is in the middle of something delicate, even while handling another interrupt. Windows needs rules for what may interrupt what. ## IRQLs Each processor has a current **IRQL** (interrupt request level). Code at a given IRQL can only be interrupted by something at a **higher** level. The levels that matter for drivers: | IRQL | Runs | May wait? | May touch paged memory? | Scheduler can switch thread? | |---|---|---|---|---| | **PASSIVE_LEVEL** (0) | Normal threads: all user code, most driver code, `DriverEntry`, most dispatch routines | Yes | Yes | Yes | | **APC_LEVEL** (1) | Asynchronous procedure calls, some file system code | Limited | Yes | Yes | | **DISPATCH_LEVEL** (2) | The scheduler itself, **DPCs**, code holding a **spin lock** | **No** | **No** | No: the thread keeps the processor | | **DIRQL** (3 and up) | Device interrupt service routines | No | No | No | The two crucial rules for DISPATCH_LEVEL and above: 1. **No waiting.** The scheduler runs at DISPATCH_LEVEL, so code at that level or above cannot be switched out. Waiting on an event or a mutex there would wait forever, so it is forbidden. 2. **No paged memory.** A page fault may need to wait for the disk (lesson 15.04), which is impossible at DISPATCH_LEVEL. Touching paged memory there crashes the machine with bug check `IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL` (`0xA`) or `DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL` (`0xD1`), the most famous blue screens, usually caused by a driver. The practice task encodes these rules as a checker. ## DPCs: doing the work later An ISR runs at a high IRQL, blocking everything below, so it must be very short: acknowledge the device and note what happened. The rest of the work goes into a **deferred procedure call** (DPC), queued by the ISR and run soon after at DISPATCH_LEVEL, where other device interrupts can still get through. Work that needs to wait or touch paged memory goes one step further down, into a **work item** that runs in a system thread at PASSIVE_LEVEL. ```mermaid flowchart LR I["Interrupt
ISR at DIRQL:
acknowledge, queue DPC"] --> D["DPC at DISPATCH_LEVEL:
process the data,
complete IRPs"] D --> W["Work item at PASSIVE_LEVEL:
anything that waits or
uses paged memory"] ``` ## Spin locks Lesson 6.06's mutexes make a waiting thread sleep, which is impossible at DISPATCH_LEVEL. For data shared with DPCs or ISRs, drivers use **spin locks**: - Acquiring a spin lock **raises the IRQL to DISPATCH_LEVEL** (so the holder cannot be preempted on its processor), then **spins** (busy-waits) until the lock is free, in case another processor holds it. - Code holding a spin lock therefore follows every DISPATCH_LEVEL rule: no waiting, no paged memory, and should hold it for only a few microseconds, because other processors may be spinning. ```cpp-norun KIRQL old; KeAcquireSpinLock(&m_lock, &old); // IRQL is now DISPATCH_LEVEL m_queue.push(item); // short, non-paged work only KeReleaseSpinLock(&m_lock, old); // back to the previous IRQL ``` For data used only at PASSIVE_LEVEL, drivers use waiting locks such as fast mutexes or executive resources instead. ## Finding out the current IRQL `KeGetCurrentIrql()` returns it. Well-written drivers assert their assumptions: `PAGED_CODE()` at the top of pageable functions checks the IRQL is below DISPATCH_LEVEL, and Driver Verifier (lesson 15.07) adds checks that catch IRQL mistakes immediately rather than in rare situations. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Waiting at DISPATCH_LEVEL > Including while holding a spin lock. It hangs or bug-checks the machine. > [!warning] Touching paged memory or calling pageable code at DISPATCH_LEVEL > Works until the page is paged out; then `IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL`. > [!warning] Long work in an ISR or under a spin lock > Everything else on that processor, and processors spinning for the lock, waits. Defer to a DPC or a work item. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What two things are forbidden at DISPATCH_LEVEL and above? - Allocating memory and returning values + Waiting, and touching paged memory or calling pageable code - Reading registers and calling functions - Using integers and using pointers > The scheduler and the page-fault handler cannot run there, so a wait or page fault cannot be serviced. ? How is work split between an ISR, a DPC and a work item? - The ISR does everything; DPCs and work items are for logging + ISR does the minimum, the DPC the main work, a work item what must wait - The work item runs first, then the DPC, then the ISR - All three run at the same IRQL in different threads > Each step down lowers the IRQL, allowing more but giving up urgency. The ISR runs at device IRQL, the DPC at DISPATCH_LEVEL, and the work item at PASSIVE_LEVEL. ? What is the difference between a spin lock and a mutex? - A spin lock is for user mode, a mutex for kernel mode - They are identical, except spin locks have shorter names - A mutex raises the IRQL; a spin lock lowers it + A spin lock busy-waits at DISPATCH_LEVEL; a mutex sleeps > Sleeping is impossible at DISPATCH_LEVEL, which is why code there must spin instead. Spin locks are only for very short work but can be used with DPCs and ISRs; a mutex only works at low IRQL. ? At which IRQL do normal threads, including `DriverEntry`, run? + PASSIVE_LEVEL - DISPATCH_LEVEL - DIRQL > Everything that may wait and use paged memory runs at PASSIVE_LEVEL. ? Why can code at DISPATCH_LEVEL not wait on an event? - Events do not exist in the kernel + The scheduler cannot switch it out to let it wait - It would use too much memory > Waiting there would hang that processor. ? What does acquiring a spin lock do to the IRQL? - Lowers it to PASSIVE_LEVEL - Nothing; IRQL is unchanged + Raises it to DISPATCH_LEVEL > So all DISPATCH_LEVEL rules apply while holding it. ? What is a DPC for? + An interrupt's follow-up work, so the ISR is short - Waiting for a user-mode thread - Loading a driver > Work that must wait goes further down, to a work item at PASSIVE_LEVEL. ```
ideas:
- Read the WDK documentation page "Managing Hardware Priorities" and its IRQL table.
- Look up bug checks `0xA` and `0xD1` in the Bug Check Code Reference and read their parameters.
- In lesson 16.02's driver, add `KdPrint` lines showing `KeGetCurrentIrql()` in `DriverEntry` and in a dispatch routine.

cards.q: What two things are forbidden at DISPATCH_LEVEL and above?
cards.a:
Waiting, and touching paged memory or calling pageable code

The scheduler and the page-fault handler cannot run there, so a wait or page fault cannot be serviced.

cards.q: How is work split between an ISR, a DPC and a work item?
cards.a:
ISR does the minimum, the DPC the main work, a work item what must wait

Each step down lowers the IRQL, allowing more but giving up urgency. The ISR runs at device IRQL, the DPC at DISPATCH_LEVEL, and the work item at PASSIVE_LEVEL.

cards.q: What is the difference between a spin lock and a mutex?
cards.a:
A spin lock busy-waits at DISPATCH_LEVEL; a mutex sleeps

Sleeping is impossible at DISPATCH_LEVEL, which is why code there must spin instead. Spin locks are only for very short work but can be used with DPCs and ISRs; a mutex only works at low IRQL.

cards.q: At which IRQL do normal threads, including `DriverEntry`, run?
cards.a:
PASSIVE_LEVEL

Everything that may wait and use paged memory runs at PASSIVE_LEVEL.

cards.q: Why can code at DISPATCH_LEVEL not wait on an event?
cards.a:
The scheduler cannot switch it out to let it wait

Waiting there would hang that processor.

cards.q: What does acquiring a spin lock do to the IRQL?
cards.a:
Raises it to DISPATCH_LEVEL

So all DISPATCH_LEVEL rules apply while holding it.

An interrupt's follow-up work, so the ISR is short

Work that must wait goes further down, to a work item at PASSIVE_LEVEL.
